claim: The human visual system is tasked with recovering the different physical sources of optical structure that generate our retinal images.
source: The human visual system is tasked with recovering the different physical sources of optical structure that generate our retinal images.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about visual system function presented in the abstract.

claim: Fully focused surface shading can be misperceived as defocused.
source: We show that fully focused surface shading can be misperceived as defocused and that optical blur can be misattributed to the material properties and shape of surfaces.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, particularly Experiments 1 and 3.

claim: Optical blur can be misattributed to the material properties and shape of surfaces.
source: We show that fully focused surface shading can be misperceived as defocused and that optical blur can be misattributed to the material properties and shape of surfaces.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 4 showing misperceptions of gloss and 3D shape.

claim: These misperceptions depend on the relationship between shading gradients and sharp contours.
source: We further reveal how these misperceptions depend on the relationship between shading gradients and sharp contours, and conclude that computations of blur are inherently linked to computations of surface shape, material, and illumination.
evidence: This is supported by experimental manipulations of contour-shading relationships across all experiments.

claim: Computations of blur are inherently linked to computations of surface shape, material, and illumination.
source: We further reveal how these misperceptions depend on the relationship between shading gradients and sharp contours, and conclude that computations of blur are inherently linked to computations of surface shape, material, and illumination.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the pattern of results across all experiments showing interdependence of these perceptual properties.

claim: An image of a surface is a product of its three-dimensional (3D) shape, the reflectance and transmittance behavior of its material, the surrounding light sources (the 'light field'), and the focal parameters of the imaging lens.
source: An image of a surface is a product of its three-dimensional (3D) shape, the reflectance and transmittance behavior of its material, the surrounding light sources (the 'light field'), and the focal parameters of the imaging lens.
evidence: This is established knowledge about image formation in computer vision and visual perception.

claim: Eyes that utilize refraction to generate a focused image are subject to depth of field defocus, which causes some image regions to be blurred.
source: Eyes that utilize refraction to generate a focused image are subject to depth of field defocus, which causes some image regions to be blurred.
evidence: This is established knowledge about optical properties of eyes.

claim: There has been a significant body of research into cues that affect the severity of perceived blur.
source: Although there has been a significant body of research into cues that affect the severity of perceived blur (Ciuffreda et al., 2006; Crete et al., 2007; Ferzli and Karam, 2006; Pentland, 1987; Tadmor and Tolhurst, 1994; Webster et al., 2002) and the role of depth of field defocus as a cue to depth (Held et al., 2010; Marshall et al., 1996; Mather, 1996; Mather, 1997; Mather and Smith, 2000; Mather and Smith, 2002; O'Shea et al., 1997; Watt et al., 2005), it is still unknown how the visual system distinguishes blur from environmental sources of low spatial frequency image structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Depth of field defocus serves as a cue to depth.
source: Although there has been a significant body of research into cues that affect the severity of perceived blur (Ciuffreda et al., 2006; Crete et al., 2007; Ferzli and Karam, 2006; Pentland, 1987; Tadmor and Tolhurst, 1994; Webster et al., 2002) and the role of depth of field defocus as a cue to depth (Held et al., 2010; Marshall et al., 1996; Mather, 1996; Mather, 1997; Mather and Smith, 2000; Mather and Smith, 2002; O'Shea et al., 1997; Watt et al., 2005), it is still unknown how the visual system distinguishes blur from environmental sources of low spatial frequency image structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: It is still unknown how the visual system distinguishes blur from environmental sources of low spatial frequency image structure.
source: Although there has been a significant body of research into cues that affect the severity of perceived blur (Ciuffreda et al., 2006; Crete et al., 2007; Ferzli and Karam, 2006; Pentland, 1987; Tadmor and Tolhurst, 1994; Webster et al., 2002) and the role of depth of field defocus as a cue to depth (Held et al., 2010; Marshall et al., 1996; Mather, 1996; Mather, 1997; Mather and Smith, 2000; Mather and Smith, 2002; O'Shea et al., 1997; Watt et al., 2005), it is still unknown how the visual system distinguishes blur from environmental sources of low spatial frequency image structure.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: The computational problem of discriminating optical defocus from environmental sources of low frequency structure does not appear to have been explicitly addressed previously.
source: The computational problem of discriminating optical defocus from environmental sources of low frequency structure does not appear to have been explicitly addressed previously.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' review of the literature.

claim: The surface depicted in Figure 1 was created by illuminating a smooth (i.e., differentiable) Lambertian ('matte') surface with a collimated light source.
source: Consider the surface depicted in Figure 1, which was created by illuminating a smooth (i.e., differentiable) Lambertian ('matte') surface with a collimated light source.
evidence: This describes the stimulus creation method for Figure 1.

claim: The surface in Figure 1 has shallow surface relief to avoid the formation of sharp attached shadows.
source: The surface has shallow surface relief to avoid the formation of sharp attached shadows and is viewed along the axis of relief to avoid the formation of self-occluding contours.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the stimulus.

claim: The surface in Figure 1 is viewed along the axis of relief to avoid the formation of self-occluding contours.
source: The surface has shallow surface relief to avoid the formation of sharp attached shadows and is viewed along the axis of relief to avoid the formation of self-occluding contours.
evidence: This describes a design feature of the stimulus.

claim: Although rendered as a fully focused surface, the image in Figure 1 elicits a strong perception of blur.
source: Although rendered as a fully focused surface, this image elicits a strong perception of blur; while some 3D shape from shading may be perceived, the surface appears 'contaminated' by optical defocus.
evidence: This is an informal observation about the perceptual experience of Figure 1.

claim: The perceptual conflation of low frequency shading gradients and optical focus does not appear to have been previously reported.
source: The perceptual conflation of low frequency shading gradients and optical focus does not appear to have been previously reported.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' review of the literature.

claim: Most research into the perception of shading has attempted to understand how shading provides information about 3D shape using images where it was assumed or somehow 'known' that the intensity gradients were caused by focused patterns of shading.
source: Most research into the perception of shading has attempted to understand how shading provides information about 3D shape using images where it was assumed or somehow 'known' that the intensity gradients were caused by focused patterns of shading.
evidence: This characterizes prior research approaches in the field.

claim: Most previous work on shape from shading has studied images that contained sharp contours generated by either smooth self-occlusions or abrupt bounding contours.
source: Most previous work on shape from shading has studied images that contained sharp contours generated by either smooth self-occlusions or abrupt bounding contours (e.g. Horn and Brooks, 1989; Koenderink et al., 2001; Mingolla and Todd, 1986; Pentland, 1984; Ramachandran, 1988; Todd et al., 1996), while experiments that have used 'terrain' surfaces similar to Figure 1 have predominantly been investigations of illumination perception (Koenderink et al., 2004; Koenderink et al., 2007).
evidence: This characterizes prior research with citations.

claim: Experiments that have used 'terrain' surfaces similar to Figure 1 have predominantly been investigations of illumination perception.
source: Most previous work on shape from shading has studied images that contained sharp contours generated by either smooth self-occlusions or abrupt bounding contours (e.g. Horn and Brooks, 1989; Koenderink et al., 2001; Mingolla and Todd, 1986; Pentland, 1984; Ramachandran, 1988; Todd et al., 1996), while experiments that have used 'terrain' surfaces similar to Figure 1 have predominantly been investigations of illumination perception (Koenderink et al., 2004; Koenderink et al., 2007).
evidence: This characterizes prior research with citations.

claim: The visual system may exploit sharp contours in generating percepts of focus when viewing low frequency shading gradients.
source: This suggests that the visual system may exploit sharp contours in generating percepts of focus when viewing low frequency shading gradients.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the pattern of prior research.

claim: It should be possible to eliminate the perception of illusory blur in Figure 1 by introducing sharp bounding contours.
source: If so, it should be possible to eliminate the perception of illusory blur in Figure 1 by introducing sharp bounding contours.
evidence: This is a testable prediction based on the hypothesis about sharp contours.

claim: The image in Figure 2A was generated by intersecting the surface in Figure 1 with a gray plane parallel to the direction of its relief and occluding all surface regions beyond the depth of that plane.
source: The image on the left (2A) was generated by intersecting the surface in Figure 1 with a gray plane parallel to the direction of its relief and occluding all surface regions beyond the depth of that plane (a particular form of 'planar cut' dubbed a 'level cut').
evidence: This describes the method used to create Figure 2A.

claim: The manipulation in Figure 2A enhances the perceived 3D shape of the surface and completely eliminates the perception of blur.
source: Informal observation suggests that this manipulation enhances the perceived 3D shape of the surface and completely eliminates the perception of blur.
evidence: This is an informal observation about the perceptual effect of the manipulation.

claim: The contour in Figure 2A appears to be unambiguously 'owned' by (attached to) the shading gradients rather than the homogeneous gray regions.
source: Note also that the contour appears to be unambiguously 'owned' by (attached to) the shading gradients rather than the homogeneous gray regions.
evidence: This is an informal observation about border ownership perception.

claim: The image in Figure 2B was created by treating the gray regions in Figure 2A as parts of a single gray 'mask' and rotating it 180 degrees over the shaded surface.
source: Now consider the image in Figure 2B, which was created by treating the gray regions in Figure 2A as parts of a single gray 'mask' and rotating it 180 degrees over the shaded surface.
evidence: This describes the method used to create Figure 2B.

claim: Figure 2B contains the exact same contours as Figure 2A, but the gray regions occlude different portions of the shaded surface.
source: This image contains the exact same contours as Figure 2A, but the gray regions occlude different portions of the shaded surface.
evidence: This describes a key property of the stimulus manipulation.

claim: The perception of shape from shading is enhanced in Figure 2A.
source: First, whereas the perceived shape from shading is enhanced in Figure 2A, the perception of shape from shading is impaired by the contours in Figure 2B.
evidence: This is an informal observation comparing the two figures.

claim: The perception of shape from shading is impaired by the contours in Figure 2B.
source: First, whereas the perceived shape from shading is enhanced in Figure 2A, the perception of shape from shading is impaired by the contours in Figure 2B.
evidence: This is an informal observation comparing the two figures.

claim: The border ownership of the contour in Figure 2B is ambiguous.
source: A second difference is that the border ownership of the contour in Figure 2B is ambiguous; whereas the contours in Figure 2A appear unambiguously attached to the shading gradients, the contours in Figure 2B can appear attached to either side.
evidence: This is an informal observation about border ownership perception.

claim: The contours in Figure 2A appear unambiguously attached to the shading gradients.
source: A second difference is that the border ownership of the contour in Figure 2B is ambiguous; whereas the contours in Figure 2A appear unambiguously attached to the shading gradients, the contours in Figure 2B can appear attached to either side.
evidence: This is an informal observation about border ownership perception.

claim: The contours in Figure 2B can appear attached to either side.
source: A second difference is that the border ownership of the contour in Figure 2B is ambiguous; whereas the contours in Figure 2A appear unambiguously attached to the shading gradients, the contours in Figure 2B can appear attached to either side.
evidence: This is an informal observation about border ownership perception.

claim: The way the border ownership is perceived in Figure 2B can have a dramatic impact on how the gradients are perceived.
source: The way the border ownership is perceived can have a dramatic impact on how the gradients are perceived.
evidence: This is an informal observation about the relationship between border ownership and gradient perception.

claim: When the contours in Figure 2B appear attached to the shading gradients, the gradients are perceived as unstructured 2D 'noise' without any clear sense of 3D shape or optical focus.
source: When the contours appear attached to the shading gradients, the gradients are perceived as unstructured 2D 'noise' (such as variations in pigment) without any clear sense of 3D shape or optical focus.
evidence: This is an informal observation about perception under one interpretation.

claim: When the contours in Figure 2B appear attached to the gray mask, the shaded surface appears as a partially occluded shaded surface that is just as blurred as the surface in Figure 1.
source: But when the contours appear attached to the gray mask, the shaded surface appears as a partially occluded shaded surface that is just as blurred as the surface in Figure 1.
evidence: This is an informal observation about perception under the alternative interpretation.

claim: Image intensity at the contour in Figure 2A varies as an approximate cosine function of orientation.
source: The plot beneath reveals how image intensity at the contour varies as an approximate cosine function of orientation.
evidence: This is shown in the plot below Figure 2A.

claim: The rotation in Figure 2B has a destructive effect on the systematic covariation between contour orientation and image intensity.
source: The plot below the image reveals the destructive effect of this rotation on the systematic covariation between contour orientation and image intensity.
evidence: This is shown in the plot below Figure 2B.

claim: The perceived focus and enhanced perception of 3D shape in level cut images arises because they approximate the geometric and photometric image properties generated by smooth self-occluding contours.
source: We suggest here that the perceived focus and enhanced perception of 3D shape arises because the level cut images approximate the geometric and photometric image properties generated by smooth self-occluding contours.
evidence: This is the authors' theoretical explanation for the observed effects.

claim: There are two constraints that play a causal role in eliciting the perception of focus in images of shaded surfaces: photogeometric constraints that arise generically along smooth self-occlusions; and the attachment of shading gradients to convex surfaces.
source: More specifically, we will argue that there are two constraints that play a causal role in eliciting the perception of focus in images of shaded surfaces: photogeometric constraints that arise generically along smooth self-occlusions; and the attachment of shading gradients to convex surfaces.
evidence: This is the authors' theoretical framework for explaining the results.

claim: Both shading intensity and bounding contour shape depend on the same environmental property – the local 3D shape of the surface – and are therefore inherently linked.
source: Both shading intensity and bounding contour shape depend on the same environmental property – the local 3D shape of the surface – and are therefore inherently linked.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the relationship between surface geometry and image properties.

claim: The local slant of a smooth self-occluding contour relative to the observer is constant (approximately 90 degrees).
source: First, it is known that the 3D shape along a smooth self-occluding rim can be derived from its 2D image contour: the local slant of the contour relative to the observer (i.e., how much it deviates from fronto-parallel) is constant (approximately 90 degrees), and the tilt of the surface (the direction in which it slants away from the observer) is specified by the orientation of the rim's image contour (Barrow and Tenenbaum, 1978).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work.

claim: The tilt of the surface at a smooth self-occluding rim is specified by the orientation of the rim's image contour.
source: First, it is known that the 3D shape along a smooth self-occluding rim can be derived from its 2D image contour: the local slant of the contour relative to the observer (i.e., how much it deviates from fronto-parallel) is constant (approximately 90 degrees), and the tilt of the surface (the direction in which it slants away from the observer) is specified by the orientation of the rim's image contour (Barrow and Tenenbaum, 1978).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work.

claim: Local 3D surface orientation is primarily responsible for shading intensity.
source: Second, it is known that local 3D surface orientation is primarily responsible for shading intensity (Horn and Brooks, 1989), subject to some modification by vignetting and/or interreflections (Langer and Zucker, 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work.

claim: For a Lambertian surface illuminated by a collimated light source, intensity will decline as a cosine function of contour orientation relative to the brightest point along the contour.
source: The mutual dependence of contour orientation and shading intensity on the same local 3D surface orientation causes shading to covary with the orientation of the rim's projected image contour: for a Lambertian surface illuminated by a collimated light source, intensity will decline as a cosine function of contour orientation relative to the brightest point along the contour (i.e., the orientation most closely aligned with the illumination direction).
evidence: This is derived from the physics of Lambertian reflectance and surface geometry.

claim: The orientation-intensity covariation relationship holds exactly for surfaces illuminated by collimated light sources.
source: This relationship holds exactly for surfaces illuminated by collimated light sources (see Materials and methods), and we have previously shown that it is statistically robust in natural light fields that contain multiple sources of illumination (Marlow et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by mathematical derivation in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The orientation-intensity covariation is statistically robust in natural light fields that contain multiple sources of illumination.
source: This relationship holds exactly for surfaces illuminated by collimated light sources (see Materials and methods), and we have previously shown that it is statistically robust in natural light fields that contain multiple sources of illumination (Marlow et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by prior work by the authors.

claim: The covariation of contour orientation and intensity along smooth self-occluding rims generalizes to other types of bounding contours such as 'planar cuts'.
source: The covariation of contour orientation and intensity along smooth self-occluding rims generalizes to other types of bounding contours that have been shown to affect perceived shape from shading, such as 'planar cuts' (i.e., contours formed by 'slicing' a shaded surface with a plane; Marlow et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by prior work by the authors.

claim: The level cut image in Figure 2A is one example of a planar cut.
source: The level cut image in Figure 2A is one example of a planar cut.
evidence: This identifies the stimulus type.

claim: Figure 2A exhibits a clear cosine-like relationship between contour orientation and shading intensity.
source: Note that Figure 2A exhibits a clear cosine-like relationship, whereas Figure 2B exhibits no covariation at all.
evidence: This is shown in the plot below Figure 2A.

claim: Figure 2B exhibits no covariation between contour orientation and shading intensity.
source: Note that Figure 2A exhibits a clear cosine-like relationship, whereas Figure 2B exhibits no covariation at all.
evidence: This is shown in the plot below Figure 2B.

claim: The orientation-intensity covariation is generally weaker for planar cuts than for self-occluding rims.
source: However, this covariation is generally weaker for planar cuts than for self-occluding rims: more than one 3D surface orientation can generate the same 2D contour orientation, which means that identically oriented planar cut segments can project different shading intensities in the image (as can be seen upon close examination of Figure 2A).
evidence: This is explained by the geometric properties of planar cuts.

claim: Planar cuts exhibit a robust orientation-intensity covariation (apart from a few degenerate cases).
source: Nonetheless, we previously showed that planar cuts exhibit a robust orientation-intensity covariation (apart from a few degenerate cases; Marlow et al., 2019), which suggests that this covariation could provide a reliable cue that the visual system uses to identify the bounding contours of shaded surfaces.
evidence: This is supported by prior work by the authors.

claim: The orientation-intensity covariation could provide a reliable cue that the visual system uses to identify the bounding contours of shaded surfaces.
source: Nonetheless, we previously showed that planar cuts exhibit a robust orientation-intensity covariation (apart from a few degenerate cases; Marlow et al., 2019), which suggests that this covariation could provide a reliable cue that the visual system uses to identify the bounding contours of shaded surfaces.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the properties of planar cuts.

claim: The level cut images in Figure 2A and smooth self-occlusions are both globally convex.
source: The second property that links the level cut image in Figure 2A to images containing smooth self-occlusions is that they are both globally convex (Koenderink, 1984).
evidence: This is a geometric property of the stimuli.

claim: The level cut surface in Figure 2C is inherently ambiguous: it can be perceived as a convex surface illuminated from below or as a concave surface illuminated from above.
source: This stimulus exhibits the same orientation-intensity covariation, but is inherently ambiguous: it can be perceived as a convex surface illuminated from below or as a concave surface illuminated from above (e.g. Ramachandran, 1988; see Liu and Todd, 2004).
evidence: This is an informal observation about the bistable perception of Figure 2C.

claim: There is a bias to perceive the illumination as coming from above.
source: There are two well-established biases that determine how such ambiguities are resolved: a bias to perceive the illumination as coming from above (Belhumeur et al., 1999; Koenderink et al., 2001) and a bias to perceive surfaces as convex (Hill and Bruce, 1994; Langer and Bülthoff, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work.

claim: There is a bias to perceive surfaces as convex.
source: There are two well-established biases that determine how such ambiguities are resolved: a bias to perceive the illumination as coming from above (Belhumeur et al., 1999; Koenderink et al., 2001) and a bias to perceive surfaces as convex (Hill and Bruce, 1994; Langer and Bülthoff, 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work.

claim: The convexity and illumination biases are aligned in Figure 2A.
source: These two biases are aligned in Figure 2a, which is presumably why this surface is perceived as a stable convex surface illuminated from above.
evidence: This is an inference about why Figure 2A appears unambiguous.

claim: The convexity and illumination biases are in conflict in Figure 2C.
source: However, these biases are in conflict in Figure 2C, causing some perceptual bistability.
evidence: This is an inference about why Figure 2C appears bistable.

claim: Perceived focus in Figure 2C depends on the perceived convexity or concavity of the surface.
source: Informal observations suggest that perceived focus depends on the perceived convexity or concavity of the surface.
evidence: This is an informal observation about the relationship between perceived shape and focus.

claim: When the surface in Figure 2C appears convex, no clear percept of blur is experienced.
source: When the surface appears convex, no clear percept of blur is experienced; but when it appears concave, the surface appears blurred.
evidence: This is an informal observation about perceived focus under different interpretations.

claim: When the surface in Figure 2C appears concave, the surface appears blurred.
source: When the surface appears convex, no clear percept of blur is experienced; but when it appears concave, the surface appears blurred.
evidence: This is an informal observation about perceived focus under different interpretations.

claim: The strength of the orientation-intensity covariation along the contours is not the sole determinant of the perception of shading, focus, and contour attachment.
source: This implies that the strength of the orientation-intensity covariation along the contours is not the sole determinant of the perception of shading, focus, and contour attachment; the convexity of the surface is also critical.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects observed in Figures 2A and 2C.

claim: The convexity of the surface is critical for the perception of shading, focus, and contour attachment.
source: This implies that the strength of the orientation-intensity covariation along the contours is not the sole determinant of the perception of shading, focus, and contour attachment; the convexity of the surface is also critical.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects observed in Figures 2A and 2C.

claim: Photogeometric cues along smooth self-occlusions and planar cuts of 1D luminance profiles provide information that predicts when identical luminance gradients are perceived as surface shading of 3D surfaces.
source: Our previous work showed that photogeometric cues along smooth self-occlusions and planar cuts of 1D luminance profiles provide information that predicts when identical luminance gradients are perceived as surface shading of 3D surfaces.
evidence: This summarizes prior work by the authors.

claim: All observers perceived the 'convex' level cut surfaces as convex bumps on all trials in Experiment 1.
source: All observers perceived the 'convex' level cut surfaces as convex bumps on all trials (first plot in Figure 3B)
evidence: This is a result from Experiment 1.

claim: The gradients occluded by rotated masks in Experiment 1 were most likely to be perceived as neither bumps nor dents.
source: whereas the gradients occluded by rotated masks were most likely to be perceived as neither bumps nor dents (third and fourth plots in Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a result from Experiment 1.

claim: The convex level cut masks were the only stimuli in Experiment 1 that were perceived as (equally) fully focused.
source: which suggests that the convex level cut masks were the only stimuli that were perceived as (equally) fully focused.
evidence: This is an inference from the pattern of results in Experiment 1.

claim: The effects of the different contours on perceived focus are mediated by the perception of convexity.
source: The data suggest that the effects of the different contours on perceived focus are mediated by the perception of convexity, which is strongest when the contours exhibit an orientation-intensity covariation with the shading and the convex interpretation is consistent with percepts of top-down illumination.
evidence: This is an inference from the pattern of results in Experiment 1.

claim: Contours generate stronger cues to contour attachment when they bound surfaces regions that appear convex.
source: This finding supports our informal observation from Figure 2: contours generate stronger cues to contour attachment when they bound surfaces regions that appear convex, and these contours are therefore more likely to propagate focus cues (produced by their sharpness) to the shaded surface.
evidence: This is an inference from the results of Experiment 1.

claim: Prior studies using globally convex shaded 3D shapes have not observed any illusory gradient blur because the self-occluding contours of these stimuli exhibit a strong orientation-intensity covariation and bound surface regions that have convex curvature.
source: This may also explain why prior studies using globally convex shaded 3D shapes have not observed any illusory gradient blur: the self-occluding contours of these stimuli not only exhibit a strong orientation-intensity covariation (Marlow et al., 2019) but also necessarily bound surface regions that have convex curvature in at least one direction.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current results to prior literature.

claim: 3D shape percepts monotonically decreased in strength as a function of increasing ribbon noise in Experiment 2.
source: The results confirm our informal experience of Figure 4: 3D shape percepts monotonically decreased in strength as a function of increasing ribbon noise (left plot in Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from Experiment 2.

claim: The effect of ribbon noise on perceived 3D shape strength in Experiment 2 was mediated by the amount of orientation-intensity covariation present in the images.
source: Further analysis revealed that this effect was mediated by the amount of orientation-intensity covariation present in the images: mean perceived 3D shape strength also decreased monotonically with the value of the Pearson correlation coefficient when the correlations measured from all presented stimuli were sorted into bins of width 0.1 (right plot in Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from Experiment 2.

claim: The three stimuli with sharp level cut contours in Experiment 3 were perceived as the most focused, even when the peaks of the surface were actually blurred by moderate or severe foreground defocus.
source: The data reveal that defocus blur can be misperceived as shading: the three stimuli with sharp level cut contours (i.e.the level cut condition with no blur or foreground blur) were perceived as the most focused, even when the peaks of the surface were actually blurred by moderate or severe foreground defocus.
evidence: This is a result from Experiment 3.

claim: The presence or absence of sharp contours attached to shading gradients can induce both misperceptions of optical focus or defocus when they exhibit a systematic intensity-orientation covariation.
source: These results demonstrate that the presence or absence of sharp contours attached to shading gradients can induce both misperceptions of optical focus or defocus (respectively) when they exhibit a systematic intensity-orientation covariation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results of Experiment 3.

claim: The transformations in perceived 3D shape in the foreground blur condition of Experiment 4 involve a systematic reduction in ridge curvature, height, and position.
source: The transformations in perceived 3D shape in the foreground blur condition involve a systematic reduction in ridge curvature, height, and position, which suggests that these perceptual distortions were not simply caused by a loss of information.
evidence: This is observed in the shape profiles in Figure 11.

claim: Observers partially misattributed the change in gradient structure induced by foreground blur to a reduction in surface curvature in Experiment 4.
source: As with perceived gloss, these findings indicate that observers partially misattributed the change in gradient structure induced by foreground blur to a reduction in surface curvature.
evidence: This is an inference from the shape results in Experiment 4.

claim: Misperceptions of optical defocus are closely coupled with misperceptions of surface properties that also contribute to the smoothness of image gradients.
source: Taken together, the results of the three tasks in Experiment 4 reveal that misperceptions of optical defocus are closely coupled with misperceptions of surface properties that also contribute to the smoothness of image gradients.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of Experiment 4.

claim: When the level cut contours in Experiment 4 were defocused by background blur, observers accurately reported a decrease in image focus.
source: When these contours were defocused by background blur, observers accurately reported a decrease in image focus, but when the ridge was defocused by foreground blur, the largest perceptual changes were instead in material (less gloss) and shape (less curvature).
evidence: This summarizes the pattern of results in Experiment 4.

claim: When the ridge in Experiment 4 was defocused by foreground blur, the largest perceptual changes were in material (less gloss) and shape (less curvature).
source: When these contours were defocused by background blur, observers accurately reported a decrease in image focus, but when the ridge was defocused by foreground blur, the largest perceptual changes were instead in material (less gloss) and shape (less curvature).
evidence: This summarizes the pattern of results in Experiment 4.

claim: The visual system was directly misattributing the smoothness of the image gradients in the foreground blur conditions to the wrong physical sources.
source: This suggests that the visual system was directly misattributing the smoothness of the image gradients in the foreground blur conditions to the wrong physical sources.
evidence: This is an inference from the pattern of results in Experiment 4.

claim: The perception of optical defocus arose in all shaded stimuli that lacked sharp bounding contours consistent with geometrically-correlated contours such as self-occlusions or level (planar) cuts of the surface.
source: We found that the perception of optical defocus arose in all shaded stimuli that lacked sharp bounding contours consistent with geometrically-correlated contours such as self-occlusions or level (planar) cuts of the surface.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding across experiments.

claim: Sharp bounding contours consistent with self-occlusions or level cuts play a critical role in modulating our experience of optical defocus and 3D shape in otherwise ambiguous images of shaded surfaces.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that this class of bounding contours plays a critical role in the modulating our experience of optical defocus and 3D shape in otherwise ambiguous images of shaded surfaces.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined results of all experiments.

claim: The results of Experiment 1 confirm that the rotated level cut mask failed to generate a clear perception of gradient focus and actually interfered with the perception of 3D shape.
source: The results of Experiment 1 confirm our informal observations that the rotated level cut mask (Figure 2B) not only failed to generate a clear perception of gradient focus, they actually interfered with the perception of 3D shape.
evidence: This summarizes the results of Experiment 1.

claim: The orientation-intensity covariation strongly predicts the perception of 3D shape.
source: Our findings showed that this covariation strongly predicts the perception of 3D shape.
evidence: This is a conclusion from Experiment 2.

claim: The results of Experiment 1 support the observation that concavities appear less focused than convexities.
source: The results of Experiment 1 support our informal observations that concavities appear less focused than convexities.
evidence: This summarizes the results of Experiment 1.

claim: The intensity-orientation covariation cannot fully explain the perception of focus in images of shaded surfaces.
source: This demonstrates that the intensity-orientation covariation cannot fully explain the perception of focus in images of shaded surfaces, as identical covariation can elicit percepts of both vivid focus and moderate defocus depending on whether the shaded surface is perceived as convex or concave (respectively).
evidence: This is an inference from the results of Experiment 1.

claim: The difference in perceived focus between convex and concave surfaces may be caused by differences in perceived contour attachment in these two configurations.
source: The difference in perceived focus may be caused by differences in perceived contour attachment in these two configurations.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to explain the observed differences.

claim: The shading gradients must appear clearly attached to the sharp contour to make full use of the information its sharpness provides about optical focus.
source: This suggests that the shading gradients must appear clearly attached to the sharp contour to make full use of the information its sharpness provides about optical focus.
evidence: This is an inference from the pattern of results.

claim: The visual system has a bias to interpret abrupt discontinuities in luminance as self-occluding contours rather than sudden changes in surface orientation.
source: This result is also consistent with arguments that the visual system has a bias to interpret abrupt discontinuities in luminance as self-occluding contours rather than sudden changes in surface orientation (Howard, 1983; Liu and Todd, 2004), which may explain why the contours appear more attached to the shading (and the shading more focused) when the surface appears convex.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work.

claim: The self-occluding contours exhibited by globally convex shaded objects may explain why their shading gradients are always perceived as fully focused and vividly three-dimensional.
source: The self-occluding contours that are invariably exhibited by these stimuli may explain why their shading gradients are always perceived as fully focused and vividly three-dimensional.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current results to prior literature.

claim: Attempts to 'eliminate' self-occlusions will only impair perceived 3D shape to the extent that the orientation-intensity covariation exhibited in the image is actually reduced.
source: Our data also imply that attempts to 'eliminate' these self-occlusions will only impair perceived 3D shape to the extent that the orientation-intensity covariation exhibited in the image is actually reduced.
evidence: This is an inference from the current results.

claim: Artificially cropping a self-occluding contour out of the image may simply create a new bounding contour that still exhibits enough covariation to induce percepts of focused 3D shading.
source: Artificially cropping a self-occluding contour out of the image, for example, may simply create a new bounding contour that still exhibits enough covariation to induce percepts of focused 3D shading.
evidence: This is a hypothesis about why certain manipulations may not be effective.

claim: Manipulations that rotate shaded terrains have been found to negatively affect perceived shape more than cropping the self-occlusions of convex objects.
source: This may explain why manipulations that rotate shaded terrains (which often exhibit no self-occlusions at all; Reichel and Todd, 1990; Todd and Reichel, 1989) have been found to negatively affect perceived shape more than cropping the self-occlusions of convex objects (Fleming et al., 2004; Egan and Todd, 2015).
evidence: This connects the current results to prior findings in the literature.

claim: Manipulations involving planar cuts may be a more effective method of investigating the role of contours in surface perception in future work.
source: Our results suggest that manipulations involving planar cuts may be a more effective method of investigating the role of contours in surface perception in future work.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research based on the current findings.

claim: It has been established that relative changes in apparent blur magnitude can provide information about scene depth.
source: It has been established that relative changes in apparent blur magnitude can provide information about scene depth (Pentland, 1987) and that sharp bounding contours can resolve the depth ordering of ambiguous surfaces (Marshall et al., 1996), but to our knowledge, no prior studies have examined how the visual system distinguishes gradients produced by optical blur from gradients produced by environmental sources such as shading.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work.

claim: Sharp bounding contours can resolve the depth ordering of ambiguous surfaces.
source: It has been established that relative changes in apparent blur magnitude can provide information about scene depth (Pentland, 1987) and that sharp bounding contours can resolve the depth ordering of ambiguous surfaces (Marshall et al., 1996), but to our knowledge, no prior studies have examined how the visual system distinguishes gradients produced by optical blur from gradients produced by environmental sources such as shading.
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from prior work.

claim: No prior studies have examined how the visual system distinguishes gradients produced by optical blur from gradients produced by environmental sources such as shading.
source: It has been established that relative changes in apparent blur magnitude can provide information about scene depth (Pentland, 1987) and that sharp bounding contours can resolve the depth ordering of ambiguous surfaces (Marshall et al., 1996), but to our knowledge, no prior studies have examined how the visual system distinguishes gradients produced by optical blur from gradients produced by environmental sources such as shading.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature.

claim: Cases of source misattribution are likely difficult to produce with the 2D textures and simple contours employed in past work on focus perception.
source: Cases of source misattribution, such as those reported here, are likely difficult to produce with the 2D textures and simple contours employed in past work on focus perception.
evidence: This is an inference about why the phenomenon was not previously observed.

claim: Identical low-frequency shading gradients can be perceived as vividly focused in some contexts and highly blurred in others.
source: Our data reveal that identical low-frequency shading gradients can be perceived as vividly focused in some contexts and highly blurred in others, which implies that models of focus perception that rely entirely on local gradient features (or even the presence of sharp contours) are not sufficient.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Models of focus perception that rely entirely on local gradient features (or even the presence of sharp contours) are not sufficient.
source: Our data reveal that identical low-frequency shading gradients can be perceived as vividly focused in some contexts and highly blurred in others, which implies that models of focus perception that rely entirely on local gradient features (or even the presence of sharp contours) are not sufficient.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: Optical focus may be better characterized as a mid-level perceptual category that interacts with the visual system's estimation of other mid-level properties such as contour attachment, 3D surface orientation and curvature, surface reflectance, and scene illumination.
source: Our findings instead suggest that optical focus may be better characterized as a mid-level perceptual category that interacts with the visual system's estimation of other mid-level properties such as contour attachment, 3D surface orientation and curvature, surface reflectance, and scene illumination.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: It seems unlikely that sharp bounding contours are the sole means by which the visual system estimates the optical focus of shaded surfaces.
source: It seems unlikely, however, that sharp bounding contours are the sole means by which the visual system estimates the optical focus of shaded surfaces.
evidence: This is a speculation about the limitations of the current findings.

claim: Shaded surfaces with regions of high curvature could exhibit enough high spatial frequencies to eliminate percepts of blur.
source: Shaded surfaces with regions of high curvature could exhibit enough high spatial frequencies to eliminate percepts of blur, which could explain why some stimuli from prior studies of shading appear focused even in the absence of any contours (e.g. the 'crater' in Figure 7 of Todd et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about an alternative mechanism for perceiving focus.

claim: Specular reflections generated by low-curvature glossy surfaces have similar spatial frequency properties to high-curvature shading.
source: Specular reflections generated by low-curvature glossy surfaces also have similar spatial frequency properties to high-curvature shading (Mooney and Anderson, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by prior work by the authors.

claim: The perception of focus in Figure 12 (left panel) requires that the specular reflections appear linked to the same surface geometry as the shading gradients.
source: However, the perception of focus in this image requires that the specular reflections appear linked to the same surface geometry as the shading gradients; if the specular reflections are rotated to arbitrary positions, the shaded surface again appears blurred, and the specular reflections appear as overlaid pigment or a second, independent layer (right panel).
evidence: This is an informal observation about Figure 12.

claim: Specular reflections must respect photogeometric constraints that link the specular and diffuse components of reflectance in order to provide information about optical focus.
source: Thus, specular reflections must also respect photogeometric constraints that link the specular and diffuse components of reflectance in order to provide information about optical focus, as has been shown previously in the perception of gloss (Anderson and Kim, 2009; Kim et al., 2011; Marlow et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by prior work on gloss perception.

claim: When relevant image features (image highlights or sharp edges) are attributed to environmental sources (attached specular highlights or attached bounding contours), they simultaneously modulate the perception of environmental properties (gloss or 3D shape) and optical focus.
source: The underlying issue in both instances is source attribution: when the relevant image features (image highlights or sharp edges) are attributed to environmental sources (attached specular highlights or attached bounding contours), they simultaneously modulate the perception of environmental properties (gloss or 3D shape) and optical focus.
evidence: This is a theoretical conclusion about the role of source attribution.

claim: In general, realistic specular reflections are not optically attached to the surface.
source: Note that, in general, realistic specular reflections are not optically attached to the surface; when the depth of field is reduced, different regions of specular reflections may only remain sharp when viewed with different focal lengths, and may not be in focus at the same focal length as the attached surface shading.
evidence: This is knowledge about the optical properties of specular reflections.

claim: The visual system exploits specific forms of geometric and photometric covariation to generate percepts of optical focus and vivid surface shading, which arise generically along both smooth self-occlusions and planar cuts.
source: We showed that the visual system exploits specific forms of geometric and photometric covariation to generate percepts of optical focus and vivid surface shading, which arise generically along both smooth self-occlusions and planar cuts.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The presence or absence of intensity-orientation correlated contours is a powerful cue to focus.
source: Our results indicate that the presence or absence of intensity-orientation correlated contours is a powerful cue to focus: fully focused shaded surfaces can appear blurred in their absence, and actual defocus can be mistaken for transformations in material and shape when correlated contours are nearby.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Fully focused shaded surfaces can appear blurred in the absence of intensity-orientation correlated contours.
source: Our results indicate that the presence or absence of intensity-orientation correlated contours is a powerful cue to focus: fully focused shaded surfaces can appear blurred in their absence, and actual defocus can be mistaken for transformations in material and shape when correlated contours are nearby.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Actual defocus can be mistaken for transformations in material and shape when correlated contours are nearby.
source: Our results indicate that the presence or absence of intensity-orientation correlated contours is a powerful cue to focus: fully focused shaded surfaces can appear blurred in their absence, and actual defocus can be mistaken for transformations in material and shape when correlated contours are nearby.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: Our perceptions of material, 3D shape, and optical defocus are inherently coupled.
source: The findings reported herein provide evidence that our perceptions of material, 3D shape, and optical defocus are inherently coupled, which suggests that optical defocus perception does not occur in a completely independent visual pathway to the perception of surface and scene properties.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: Optical defocus perception does not occur in a completely independent visual pathway to the perception of surface and scene properties.
source: The findings reported herein provide evidence that our perceptions of material, 3D shape, and optical defocus are inherently coupled, which suggests that optical defocus perception does not occur in a completely independent visual pathway to the perception of surface and scene properties.
evidence: This is an inference from the finding that these perceptions are coupled.

claim: For non-Lambertian diffuse reflectance functions with roughness parameters, the falloff function will not be an exact cosine, but will at least be monotonic and continuous.
source: For non-Lambertian diffuse reflectance functions with roughness parameters (e.g. Oren and Nayar, 1993), this falloff function will not be an exact cosine, but will at least be monotonic and continuous.
evidence: This is an inference from the properties of non-Lambertian reflectance functions.

claim: Level cut contour orientation is always equal to surface tilt, but only up to a 180° ambiguity.
source: Level cut contour orientation is always equal to surface tilt, but only up to a 180° ambiguity: the adjacent surface could be convex (i.e. the 3D surface normal points out of the shaded region) or concave (i.e. the 3D surface normal points into the shaded region).
evidence: This is derived from the geometric properties of level cuts.

claim: The overall correlation between image intensity and orientation across large areas of the image is likely to remain high for level cuts.
source: The visual system is unlikely to be deterred by any small slant-induced distortions in the shape of the cosine relationship between luminance and contour orientation, which implies that Equation 3 will still approximately hold for level cuts; the overall correlation between image intensity and orientation across large areas of the image is therefore likely to remain high.
evidence: This is an inference from the mathematical analysis.
